title: WE TAUGHT THEM HOW TO GET TO HEAVEN… BUT DID WE FORGET TO TEACH THEM HOW TO FOLLOW JESUS ON EARTH?
paragraphs: WE TAUGHT THEM HOW TO GET TO HEAVEN… BUT DID WE FORGET TO TEACH THEM HOW TO FOLLOW JESUS ON EARTH?
What if one of the greatest tragedies in modern Christianity is that we have convinced people to prepare for eternity while leaving them unprepared to live as disciples of Jesus Christ today?
There is a question haunting me.
Not because I have lost faith in the Church.
But because I believe in Jesus too much to pretend that everything we call Christianity actually looks like Him.

What if someone can spend twenty years attending church, memorize the language of salvation, know exactly what to say when someone asks whether they are going to heaven… and still have almost no idea how to follow Jesus when life becomes unbearable?
What if we have taught people how to raise their hands during an altar call, but not how to surrender their pride when they get home?
What if we have taught them to sing about forgiveness on Sunday, but not how to forgive the person whose betrayal still keeps them awake on Tuesday night?
What if we have taught them to anticipate streets of gold while ignoring the brokenhearted people walking beside them on streets of concrete?
And what if the most frightening part is that we have become so accustomed to this contradiction that we barely notice it anymore?
Before you assume this is another article criticizing churches, please hear me.
This is not an attack on the Bride of Christ.
This is a plea for her to remember the voice of her Bridegroom.
Because Jesus never invited us merely to admire the destination.
He called us to follow Him along the way.
And somewhere between our sermons about heaven and our struggles here on earth, we may have forgotten how deeply those two realities belong together.
I think about the person who sits in the back of the church every Sunday.
They know when to stand. When to sit. When to say amen.
They know the songs.
They know the Scriptures printed on the screen.
But nobody knows that they cried in their car before walking into the building.
Nobody knows they are struggling with pornography, resentment, loneliness, secret debt, or a marriage that feels like two strangers sharing an address.
Nobody knows that sometimes they open their Bible, stare at the pages, and quietly wonder why following Jesus seems so much harder than everyone makes it look.
They have been told that heaven is their home.
And that is a glorious promise for those who belong to Christ.
But tonight they are still living in a house full of conflict.
Tomorrow they must return to a workplace where integrity costs something.
Next week they must face someone who wounded them.
And right now they desperately need to know what it means to walk with Jesus through all of it.
Not merely someday.
Today.
This is where the words of Jesus become almost impossible to ignore.
In Matthew 28:19–20, the risen Christ commissions His followers to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to observe everything He commanded.
The Greek text contains the word μαθητεύσατε (mathēteusate), meaning "make disciples."
Not simply gather audiences.
Not merely produce religious admirers.
Make disciples.
And the command to teach them is joined to τηρεῖν (tērein), meaning to keep, observe, or obey.
Jesus did not command His Church merely to distribute information about Him.
He commanded His Church to form people who would learn to live under His teaching.
And this matters because a person can know a great deal about Jesus without actually walking closely with Him.
You can explain the doctrine of forgiveness while nursing a grudge.
You can defend biblical marriage while neglecting your spouse.
You can argue about holiness while humiliating people online.
You can preach generosity while treating struggling people with contempt.
You can know the correct answers and still resist the Lord who gave them.
James confronts this very danger.
"But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves." (James 1:22, KJV)
That last phrase should make us uncomfortable.
Deceiving your own selves.
Not necessarily deceiving the pastor.
Not necessarily deceiving the congregation.
Yourself.
There is a kind of religious familiarity that can convince a person they are spiritually mature simply because they have heard the truth repeatedly.
But hearing about obedience is not the same as obeying.
Knowing that Jesus washed feet is not the same as humbling yourself to serve.
Knowing that Jesus loved His enemies is not the same as praying for someone who has treated you cruelly.
Knowing that Jesus trusted His Father is not the same as trusting God when your prayers seem unanswered.
And knowing that Jesus died for sinners is not the same as admitting that you still desperately need His mercy.
Perhaps this is why some of the most unsettling words in Scripture were spoken not to atheists, but to people who openly acknowledged Jesus as Lord.
"Why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?" (Luke 6:46, KJV)
Imagine hearing that question without the protection of religious familiarity.
Why do you call Me Lord?
Why do you sing to Me?
Why do you defend My name?
Why do you publicly identify yourself with Me?
But resist My words when they confront the things you refuse to surrender?
This is not a call to earn salvation through flawless performance.
That would contradict the Gospel.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of works.
And the very next verse tells us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared for us to walk in.
Notice the order.
We are not saved because we have successfully followed Jesus.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Christ, and that grace brings us into a new life in which we learn to follow Him.
Obedience is not the price we pay to purchase God's love.
It is the fruit of a life being transformed by His love.
That distinction is everything.
Because without grace, discipleship becomes religious exhaustion.
And without discipleship, our profession of grace can become an excuse for refusing transformation.
Jesus did not shed His blood merely to improve our religious vocabulary.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
To forgive.
To redeem.
To make us new.
And to teach us to walk in the freedom His sacrifice has secured.
The apostle Paul writes in Titus 2:11–12 that the grace of God brings salvation and teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives in this present world.
Did you catch that?
Grace teaches us.
Not just how to die with hope.
How to live with Christ now.
The Greek word translated "teaching" in Titus 2:12 is παιδεύουσα (paideuousa), carrying the sense of training, educating, and disciplining.
Grace is not merely a declaration that our sins can be forgiven.
Grace also trains those who belong to Christ to turn away from sin and grow in godliness.
And that training happens in the ordinary, uncomfortable places where our true character is revealed.
It happens when your child disobeys you for the fifth time and you must choose whether to respond with patience or anger.
It happens when your spouse disappoints you and you must decide whether to seek reconciliation or punish them with silence.
It happens when someone else's success exposes the envy you thought you had overcome.
It happens when nobody is watching and you must decide whether integrity is still worth practicing.
It happens when you are exhausted, misunderstood, tempted, afraid, or carrying a grief that nobody else seems to recognize.
Following Jesus is not reserved for the extraordinary moments when the worship music swells and tears fall down our faces.
It is often revealed in the quiet decisions nobody applauds.
The apology.
The confession.
The refusal to retaliate.
The honest conversation.
The unseen act of generosity.
The prayer whispered through clenched teeth.
The choice to turn away from a familiar sin and seek help instead of hiding again.
These moments may never make anyone famous.
But they matter to the Lord.
And perhaps some of us need to admit something painful.
We have become very good at celebrating Christian identity while sometimes neglecting Christian formation.
We ask people whether they have accepted Jesus.
That is an important question.
But do we also teach them how to abide in Him?
How to read Scripture faithfully rather than merely collect inspirational verses?
How to pray when they feel nothing?
How to resist temptation without pretending temptation does not exist?
How to confess sin without surrendering to despair?
How to practice justice and mercy?
How to endure suffering without assuming God has abandoned them?
How to love their neighbors when their neighbors are difficult to love?
How to handle money, power, relationships, sexuality, ambition, disappointment, and conflict under the lordship of Christ?
How to remain faithful when following Jesus costs them approval?
Because discipleship is not an optional advanced course for unusually serious Christians.
It is the life to which Jesus calls His people.
In Luke 9:23, Jesus says:
"If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." (KJV)
Daily.
That word changes the conversation.
The Greek text uses καθ’ ἡμέραν (kath’ hēmeran), meaning "day by day" or "daily."
Not only at conversion.
Not only during revival meetings.
Not only when circumstances are favorable.
Daily.
When faith feels strong.
When faith feels fragile.
When obedience brings joy.
When obedience involves sacrifice.
When you wake up grateful.
And when you wake up wondering how you will survive another day.
Jesus calls His disciples to follow Him through the ordinary rhythm of life.
But please understand something.

Taking up your cross does not mean remaining in abuse, accepting exploitation, refusing medical treatment, or believing that every form of suffering is something God requires you to endure without help.
Jesus' call is to self-denial and costly allegiance to Him, not permission for others to harm you.
And following Christ does not mean pretending to be strong when you are wounded.
Sometimes faithfulness looks like asking for help.
Sometimes it looks like telling the truth about what happened.
Sometimes it looks like seeking wise pastoral care, professional support, or safety.
Sometimes it looks like finally admitting that the image you have been maintaining is crushing the person underneath.
The Jesus who calls us to deny ourselves is also the Jesus who invites the weary and burdened to come to Him for rest (Matthew 11:28–30).
He is not a cruel taskmaster demanding that broken people manufacture perfection.
He is the Savior who receives sinners, gives rest, and transforms His people by grace.
And this is where I think about Peter.
Not the polished version we sometimes imagine.
The real Peter.
The disciple who boldly promised loyalty.
The man who believed he would stand even if everyone else fell.
The follower who drew a sword in one moment and denied knowing Jesus in another.
Imagine the sound of the rooster.
Imagine the terrible realization that you have done exactly what you insisted you would never do.
Luke 22:61 tells us that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Then Peter remembered.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
Scripture does not tell us everything that passed through Peter's mind.
But anyone who has betrayed their own convictions can recognize something of that moment.
The shame of knowing better.
The weight of having failed.
The awful question of whether your failure has become your identity.
And perhaps that is where some of you are living right now.
You have heard sermons about victory.
But you feel defeated.
You have heard testimonies about freedom.
But you are still fighting a familiar temptation.
You have heard people talk about spiritual maturity.
But you are ashamed of how easily anger, fear, envy, or bitterness still rises inside you.
You love Jesus.
And you are painfully aware of how much in your life still needs to change.
Please do not mistake conviction for the absence of hope.
Peter's story did not end beside that charcoal fire of denial.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, the risen Lord questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
The man who had denied Jesus was not beyond the reach of restoring grace.
But notice what Jesus did not do.
He did not teach Peter that failure was harmless.
He did not pretend the denial never happened.
And He did not reduce restoration to a moment of emotional relief.
He called Peter back into love, service, and faithful following.
"Follow me." (John 21:19, KJV)
Two words.
Spoken by the risen Savior to a man who knew the bitterness of failure.
Not, "Prove that you have never fallen."
Not, "Rebuild your reputation before you come near Me."
Not, "Your worst moment must define the rest of your life."
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not that sin does not matter.
Sin matters so profoundly that Christ died for our sins.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
Jesus Himself called people to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15).
But that failure does not have to be the final chapter for the person who turns to Christ.
There is forgiveness in Him.
There is reconciliation with God through Him.
There is power for a transformed life by His Spirit.
And there is a future that our past cannot purchase, destroy, or deserve.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Yet here is the part we cannot afford to miss.
Jesus did not restore Peter merely so Peter could feel better about himself.
He restored him to a life of following and serving.
The grace that lifted Peter from shame also called him forward into responsibility.
And that is what genuine discipleship does.
It does not leave people imprisoned in guilt.
But neither does it leave them comfortably unchanged.
It brings them to Jesus, again and again, until His truth begins to reshape how they live.
Perhaps the Church needs to recover this kind of patient, truthful, grace-filled discipleship.
Not just bigger crowds.
Deeper roots.
Not just powerful moments.
Faithful lives.
Not just people who can repeat the promise of eternal life.
People who are learning to embody the love of Christ in the world around them.
And please, do not misunderstand me.
We must never stop preaching heaven.
The hope of resurrection is not a distraction from Christian discipleship.
It is one of its greatest sources of courage.
Jesus promised His disciples that He was going to prepare a place for them (John 14:1–3).
Paul reminded believers that their citizenship is in heaven and that they await the Savior (Philippians 3:20).
Revelation 21 gives us a breathtaking vision of God's dwelling with His people, where death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
We need that hope.
The grieving widow needs it.
The believer enduring persecution needs it.
The parent standing beside a grave needs it.
The exhausted Christian who wonders whether suffering will ever end needs it.
Christianity without the resurrection and the promise of eternal life would not be the Gospel proclaimed by the apostles.
But biblical hope does not teach us to abandon the present.
It teaches us to live faithfully within it.
In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul spends an entire chapter defending the resurrection.
Then he concludes by urging believers to remain steadfast and abound in the work of the Lord, knowing that their labor is not in vain.
Do you see the connection?
Because resurrection is real, what we do for Christ now matters.
Because eternity is real, faithfulness today is not wasted.
Because Jesus is coming again, we have every reason to love, serve, endure, and obey while we wait.
Heaven is not an excuse to neglect the earth.
It is a promise that strengthens us to live for Christ here.
Even the prayer Jesus taught His disciples holds these realities together.
"Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven." (Matthew 6:10, KJV)
In the Greek text, the petition includes γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου (genēthētō to thelēma sou) — "let Your will be done."
That prayer is not a demand that we create heaven through human effort.
God alone brings His kingdom to its promised fullness.
But it is a prayer of surrendered allegiance.
We ask for God's will to be done, and we offer ourselves as people willing to obey it.
Not just when we die.
While we live.
So imagine what might happen if we taught discipleship with the same seriousness with which we teach the hope of heaven.
Imagine a church where a newly converted believer is not simply congratulated and then left alone to figure out the Christian life.
Imagine someone walking beside them.
Opening Scripture with them.
Teaching them to pray.
Helping them understand repentance.
Showing them how to face temptation.
Encouraging them when they stumble.
Correcting them gently when they wander.
Reminding them that salvation rests on Christ, not on their ability to maintain an impressive religious image.
Imagine children growing up seeing parents who do not merely quote Scripture, but apologize when they are wrong.
Imagine marriages where the language of grace becomes a daily practice of honesty, humility, fidelity, and forgiveness.
Imagine Christians who are known not only for the positions they defend, but for the mercy, truthfulness, courage, and love with which they live.
Imagine congregations where struggling believers can confess sin and seek help without fear of being turned into gossip.
Where the wounded are protected.
Where the poor are not forgotten.
Where leaders are accountable.
Where the Gospel is not diluted to make everyone comfortable, but neither is truth weaponized to crush the repentant.
Where holiness is pursued with humility.
Where grace is celebrated without excusing evil.
Where the name of Jesus is not merely displayed on a building but honored through the lives of His people.
Wouldn't that be a beautiful witness?
Not a perfect church.
There has never been a congregation of sinless people.
But a church continually returning to its perfect Savior.
A church willing to repent.
A church willing to learn.
A church willing to follow.
Jesus said in John 13:35 that people would recognize His disciples by their love for one another.
That is a remarkable statement.
He did not say the world would recognize us primarily by the size of our platforms, the sophistication of our arguments, or the number of religious events on our calendars.
Love.
Not sentimental approval of everything.
Not avoidance of difficult truth.
But the kind of love that flows from Christ and reflects His character.
The love that serves.
The love that speaks truth.
The love that bears burdens.
The love that refuses to turn wounded people into disposable people.
The love that remembers we were all desperate for mercy before we had anything to offer.
And perhaps this is where the question becomes deeply personal.
Because it is easy to criticize the modern Church.
It is much harder to ask whether we ourselves have been following Jesus.
So I want to ask you something.
Not as a judge standing above you.
As someone who must stand beneath the same Word.
When was the last time Scripture corrected something in your life, and you actually changed direction?
When was the last time you apologized without defending yourself?
When was the last time you prayed for someone who could do absolutely nothing for you?
When was the last time you resisted the temptation to turn someone else's failure into entertainment?
When was the last time you chose obedience over convenience?
When was the last time you opened the Bible not merely looking for reassurance, but ready to be confronted, comforted, and transformed by God's truth?
And perhaps the hardest question of all:
If someone learned what following Jesus means by watching the way you live, what would they learn about Him?
That question reaches me too.
Because I do not want to become so skilled at speaking about Jesus that I forget to sit at His feet.
I do not want to know the language of surrender while protecting the very things He is asking me to release.
I do not want to spend my life inviting people into a faith I am unwilling to practice.
And I do not want anyone reading this to confuse spiritual performance with the real Christian life.
Some days following Jesus will look like courageous public witness.
Other days it will look like quiet repentance in your bedroom.
Some days it will look like serving hundreds of people.
Other days it will look like faithfully caring for one difficult person.
Some days it will look like victory over a temptation.
Other days it will look like refusing to surrender to despair after you have fallen, confessing your sin, receiving God's mercy, and taking the next faithful step.
The Christian life is not sustained by pretending we no longer need grace.
It is sustained by remaining dependent on Christ.
Jesus says in John 15:5:
"I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing." (KJV)
Without Me.
Not without a religious reputation.
Not without an impressive testimony.
Not without a perfect social media image.
Without Me.
That is the difference between merely appearing Christian and actually abiding in Christ.
And it is why we cannot disciple people into dependence on personalities, platforms, or programs.
We must continually point them to Jesus.
Pastors are not the Vine.
Ministries are not the Vine.
Christian influencers are not the Vine.
Even the most helpful discipleship resources are not the Vine.
Christ is the Vine.
Everything else must serve the purpose of helping people know Him, trust Him, obey Him, and grow in His grace.
That conviction is also at the heart of why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a following that revolves around a human personality.
Not to replace the local church.
But to keep placing biblical truth, encouragement, conviction, and discipleship resources before people who need to hear that Jesus is still calling them.
Some of those people are believers who have grown weary.
Some are new Christians who have no idea where to begin.
Some have been wounded by religious hypocrisy and are struggling to trust again.
Some are seekers who have questions they are afraid to ask.
Some are people who have been away from church for years, quietly wondering whether the door back to God is still open.
And some are simply trying to make it through another ordinary day without losing their grip on hope.
They need more than another religious slogan.
They need the Gospel.
They need Scripture handled faithfully.
They need reminders of grace that do not erase repentance.
They need teaching that connects eternal truth with real-life obedience.
And they need to know that the invitation of Jesus is still open.
Those resources are not a substitute for Scripture, prayer, Christian fellowship, or faithful participation in a local church.
They are tools intended to help nourish those practices.
And they are available freely because spiritual growth should never be presented as something only people with money can pursue.
But making resources available, maintaining the ministry, developing new materials, and expanding its reach also involve real work and real costs.
Not because you owe this ministry a payment for God's grace.
You do not.
Those responsibilities deserve their own prayerful consideration.
But because voluntary, generous support can be one practical way of serving others for the glory of God.
The New Testament teaches that giving should be willing rather than coerced. Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver, not someone pressured into giving reluctantly.
For some, that may be an expression of generosity alongside their regular giving.
For others, sharing these resources may be the more appropriate way to help.
Both can be meaningful.
Neither purchases God's favor.
And no one should neglect essential family needs, debt obligations, or the care of others to support an online ministry.
But for those who have been looking for a tangible way to help more people encounter Scripture and grow as disciples, this is an invitation worth prayerfully considering.
The greater purpose is the work we can help sustain together.
More biblical encouragement.
More discipleship materials.
More opportunities to reach people who are searching, struggling, doubting, or learning to follow Christ.
Not merely to increase a number on a screen.
Someone who is exhausted by pretending.
Someone who thinks their repeated failures mean God is finished with them.
Someone who has mistaken church attendance for discipleship.
Someone who needs to discover that following Jesus is neither empty religious performance nor a hopeless attempt to earn salvation.
It is a life of grace, repentance, faith, obedience, and dependence on the living Christ.
Or send this privately to a person who may need encouragement but would not want their struggles discussed publicly.
Not with a polished religious answer.
With something real.
Or share one area where God is teaching you obedience right now.
Perhaps it is forgiveness.
Perhaps it is patience.
Perhaps it is honesty.
Perhaps it is learning to pray again.
Perhaps it is returning to Christ after a season of wandering.
You do not need to reveal private wounds or details you are not ready to share.
But your honest testimony may encourage someone who believes they are the only person still struggling.
And if you are exhausted, a simple "pray for me" is enough.
There is no shame in asking other believers to carry you in prayer.
Return to these Scriptures.
Examine them in context.
Pray over them.
Invite your family, your friends, the believers who feel spiritually distant, and even the people who are still exploring Christianity to follow along.
Not because a social media page can save anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But because a faithful word of Scripture, encountered at the right moment, can direct someone toward the Savior who can.
And perhaps that is how a simple act of sharing becomes an act of love.
One person reads.
One person begins asking questions.
One person opens a Bible that has been gathering dust.
One person seeks forgiveness.
One person returns to Christian fellowship.
One person realizes that they cannot continue calling Jesus Lord while refusing to listen to His words.
And one person discovers that the grace of Christ is not exhausted by the failures they have been hiding.
We cannot manufacture those outcomes.
The Holy Spirit is the One who convicts and transforms.
But we can faithfully plant and water, trusting God for the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).
And that is enough reason to keep going.
Because the goal was never simply to produce more religious content.
The goal is to make much of Jesus.
To proclaim His death and resurrection.
To call people to repentance and faith.
To help believers grow in the knowledge of His Word.
To encourage them to live as His disciples in their homes, workplaces, churches, and communities.
To remind the ashamed that forgiveness is found in Christ.
To remind the proud that they still need mercy.
To remind the weary that Jesus gives rest.
And to remind the Church that the Great Commission was never merely a command to collect decisions.
It was a command to make disciples.
There is one final image I cannot shake.
Imagine standing before Jesus after a lifetime of talking about Him.
Not before an audience.
Not before a congregation.
Not before people impressed by your biblical knowledge.
Before Him.
The One who knew your thoughts when nobody else did.
The One who saw every secret act of kindness.
The One who witnessed every hidden compromise.
The One who knew how often you stumbled and how often you returned to Him for mercy.
The One whose blood alone is sufficient to cleanse sinners.
What would matter in that moment?
Not the number of people who applauded your faith.
Not the image you maintained.
Not the religious arguments you won.
But whether your confidence was truly in Christ — the Savior whose grace calls His people into a life of following Him.
Matthew 7:21–23 contains a sobering warning that merely calling Jesus "Lord" and pointing to impressive religious activity does not guarantee that a person truly belongs to Him.
Those words are not an invitation to despair or to search for assurance in personal perfection.
They are an invitation to reject false confidence and come honestly to the real Jesus.
The Jesus who said, "Come unto me" (Matthew 11:28).
The Jesus who said, "Follow me" (Matthew 4:19).
The Jesus who said, "If ye love me, keep my commandments" (John 14:15).
The Jesus who died for our sins and rose again.
The Jesus who remains the only Savior.
And perhaps that is where this entire question finally leads us.
Are we preparing people for heaven while forgetting to teach them how to follow Jesus today?
We must not choose between those two callings.
We must preach the eternal hope secured by Christ.
And we must teach the present life of discipleship that flows from His grace.
We must proclaim justification by faith.
And we must teach sanctification by the Spirit.
We must tell people that salvation cannot be earned.
And we must tell them that saving grace is never permission to make peace with sin.
We must comfort the brokenhearted.
And we must confront the comfortable.
We must teach believers how to face death with hope.
And how to face tomorrow with faithfulness.
Because the same Jesus who promises resurrection life also calls His people to follow Him today.
So before you close this article, consider one simple question.
What is one thing Jesus has already shown you through His Word that you need to begin obeying today?
Not ten dramatic promises.
Not another temporary emotional high.
One honest step.
One conversation you have been avoiding.
One sin you need to confess.
One person you need to forgive.
One boundary you need to establish.
One act of service you have been postponing.
One decision to seek help.
One return to Scripture.
One prayer of surrender.
Not to earn His love.
But because His grace has met you, and you want your life to reflect the One who saved you.
If you have never truly trusted Christ, begin there. Turn to Him in repentance and faith. His death and resurrection, not your religious achievements, are the foundation of salvation.
If you already belong to Him but have wandered, return to Him.
If you are weary, come to Him.
If you have fallen, confess your sin and seek His mercy.
If you are growing, remain humble.
If you are teaching others, teach them to obey everything Jesus commanded.
And if you are helping build a ministry, a family, a church, or a community, never forget whose name must remain at the center.
Not ours.
His.
Because at the end of everything, the most important question is not simply whether we spent our lives talking about going to heaven.
It is whether we truly knew and followed the Savior who brings His people home.
May we never become so occupied with telling people where Jesus will take them someday that we forget to show them how to walk with Him today.
